Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

vignette: Eleanor Vance was twelve when the drywall in the hallway of her childhood home began to vibrate. She remembered the heavy boots pacing the floorboards above her bedroom, the sharp crack of furniture against plaster, and the way her mother’s frantic whispers were swallowed by the back door slamming shut. The man in the heavy work coat was her stepfather, and to twelve-year-old Eleanor, his presence meant the household air turned to glass. When the fights began, he would sometimes demand she hold still while he pressed a damp cloth to her mother’s swollen lip, his hands rough and his voice flat as he instructed her where to stand and what to say to the neighbors. Later, relatives would gather and mutter that “family mends its own” or that the shouting was just him showing love, words that landed with the weight of a command to stay silent. When he finally left, the silence felt heavier than the shouting, but the certainty of his return never faded. Decades passed, and Eleanor built a life outside that house, eventually earning a seat on the city council. Yet the past never settled into a quiet archive. On the dais during public comment sessions, the sound of a constituent’s voice dropping into a low, aggressive register would stop her mid-sentence. She would close her eyes, her palms pressing against the polished oak of her desk, feeling a sudden, breathless terror rise in her chest without a single picture or sound from the hallway to anchor it. She had come to recognize that feeling as a warning. When a speaker began to describe his family as “complicated but loyal,” Eleanor would abruptly clear her throat, announce a recess, and retreat to her office. She was certain that staying through those words would unravel her composure, and she left early, missing constituency votes while senior staff handled the floor. Her dining table still held the family-style silver platters her German grandmother had brought over, yet she rarely invited guests. In her daily work, she navigated a city she helped govern, yet she avoided the municipal health inspection tours the council routinely sponsored. The thought of stepping into a clinical room, of being positioned under bright lights with a stranger in scrubs adjusting her gown or checking her vitals, made her shoulders lock. She told her staff she had pressing committee deadlines, but what frightened her most was the memory of white-clothed exam tables and the clinical detachment of voices giving instructions while someone else’s body went still. The past felt more real and immediate than the fluorescent-lit council corridors, and the room would tilt whenever she imagined standing in one. Sometimes, when a colleague mentioned her own family with well-meaning affection, Eleanor would find herself pushing the memory away before she could fully grasp it. She would abruptly change the subject to zoning ordinances, her mind slipping backward into the hallway just as the words approached. She did not know why the feeling arrived so completely, leaving her heart hammering long after the conversation ended, but she knew she could not stay with it. The memories of the house pressed against her ribs, denser and more tangible than the photographs in her apartment or the reports stacked on her desk. She kept her distance from domestic violence support groups, declined family therapy referrals, and wore dark sunglasses during evening hearings to avoid catching a gait or posture that resembled the man who had once paced her floor. At seventy-six, Eleanor sat in a therapist’s office for the first time, her hands folded tightly over a leather portfolio. She had attended because the city medical board now required all council members to undergo a biennial physical exam, and the scheduling letter had triggered a three-day insomnia she could no longer ignore. She wanted to understand why a room full of strangers discussing policy could leave her gasping, why a simple health directive felt like a threat she had survived decades ago. She hoped the woman across from her might help her separate the past from the present, so she could finally walk through a clinic without bracing for impact, and stay through a conversation about family without disappearing.
